title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 Intrinsic vs. Post-Hoc Methods
(This section was previously called: “Categorization of XML Methods”)
There are many taxonomies in which interpretability methods can be categorized, they can be categorized according to the nature of the learning algorithm or the stage at which the model becomes interpretable into Intrinsic and Post-Hoc methods, They can also be categorized into Local and Global methods according to the scope of explanations.
Intrinsic methods indicate that the model itself is inherently interpretable by design the algorithm itself tends to be less complex and the factors affecting the decision making process are always disentangled (Molnar 2025). Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, Generalized linear models (GLMs) (Wang and Ji 2025) and Decision Trees are examples of models that are interpretable by design, they either show the importance of each feature, or come up with human readable decision rules (Miller 2019; Molnar 2025). While those models are extremely simple, efficient and interpretable they face many limitations when deployed to the real world, For example linear models can be interpreted by measuring the feature importance; by looking into the coefficient of each feature in the weight matrix (Molnar 2025). However, they are built on very strict assumptions and inductive biases such as linearity, independence, and absence of heteroscedasticity which are difficult to gurantee in the real world (Hastie et al. 2009), this limits the ability of such algorithms to capture true, non-linear patterns underlying the data or even model complex high dimensional data which limits the predictive performance of such models.
While linear models fail to model non-linear data, tree-based models come into play. They work by splitting the data multiple times according to discovered thresholds over the values of the features (Molnar 2025). Each learning algorithm uses a different criterion to grow the optimal tree. For example, ID3 measures the Information Gain criterion to find the best splits (Quinlan 1986), While CART optimizes for the Gini Impurity (Breiman et al. 1984). All tree based algorithms are capable of modeling non-linear data. Those models are Interpretable intrinsically; you can traverse the tree starting from the root to the leaf in order to find the decision in the form of sequential If-Else statements. However, due to the greedy nature of the learning algorithm it tends to increase the depth of the tree drastically leading to a trade-off between error minimization and being easily interpretable (Molnar 2025).
On the other hand, Post-Hoc methods work by reporting how an already trained model produces its predictions, For any given input it tries to provide understandable explanations for the learned decision boundaries by the more complex black-box models Molnar (2025). Post-Hoc methods can be categorized into two main categories: Model-Agnostic methods, and model model-specific methods (Arrieta et al. 2019), Where the former can be plugged into any model to explain its decision space, e.g perturbation based approaches like LIME (Ribeiro et al. 2016) and SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017) that predict how the decision space changes when the input data point is perturbed, While the latter is specific to a model architecture like analyzing attention maps in transformer networks, or gradient-based methods that look into the gradient of the input with respect to the loss function to provide pixel-level explanations like Saliency Maps (Simonyan et al. 2014), class activation maps (CAM) (Minh 2023) and it varients like GradCAMs (Selvaraju et al. 2019) in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are also used to quantify the amount of input activation conditioned on the output class to provide a heat-map for the relevant regions for the predicted class.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1.1 Linear Regression
Linear regression represents the output variable \(y\) as a linear combination of the input features \(\mathbf{X}\) weighted by the scaling coefficient matrix \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Mathematically:\[\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon},\] \[\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}, \quad \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, \quad \boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^{p}, \quad \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}.\]where \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) is called the irreducible error term, it is typically considered a random variable with zero mean and constant variance. It captures the noise, and the variations in the data that the model failed to explain using the given features, \(n\) is the number of training instances, and \(p\) is the number of features.
We can run iterative optimization using standard gradient descent algorithm (Ruder 2017) to find the betas that minimize mean squared error (MSE):\[J(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \frac{1}{2n} \left\Vert{} \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} \right\Vert{}_2^2.\] \[\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)} - \eta \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{X}^{\top} (\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)}-\mathbf{y}),\] \[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x_j} = \boldsymbol{\beta}_j,\]
Linear Regression models are inherently interpretable through their coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\). Each coefficient \(\beta_j\) quantifies the effect of the corresponding feature represented by the \(j\)-th column of the feature matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) as shown in Figure 1.1.






Figure 1.1: Linear regression correctly captures the relationship between the feature and the target. The coefficient \(\beta\) corresponds to the constant marginal effect \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x}\), making the model directly interpretable.



While Linear Regression is simple, and interpretable by design, many limitations rise from the implicit inductive biases assumed by this model (Wang and Ji 2025). First, Linear Regression models assumes a linear relationship between the input features and the target variable if the relation is not linear the learned coefficient fails to explain the effect of the feature as shown in Figure 1.2, more formally: \[\frac{\partial y}{\partial x_j} \neq \boldsymbol{\beta}_j,\]






Figure 1.2: When the underlying data distribution is non-linear, linear regression coefficients fails to explain the relationship.



Also, Linear Regression models assumes independence between features. Feature correlation can be reflected in the Gram matrix \(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\), where off-diagonal elements quantify the similarity between feature columns. Strong correlations between features introduce multicollinearity, making the estimated coefficients \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) unstable and reduces interpretability as shown in Figure 1.3.






Figure 1.3: When features are mutually collinear the explanations provided by learned coefficients becomes unstable through multiple runs. In this example we generate a correlated feature using \(x_2 = x_1 + \epsilon\), where \(\epsilon_i {\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,0.05^2)\).

title: 8  Introduction
text:
8.1 Activation-based explanations
Language models transform tokens through a sequence of learned representations before producing an output. Explainability methods study different parts of this process. Some inspect internal activations, some describe predictions using human-readable concepts, and others discover recurring patterns in the model’s representations.
This tutorial separates these approaches into three families. The boundary is useful for organizing the methods, although some techniques combine ideas from more than one family.
Activation-based explanations examine the values produced inside a model as it processes an input. They may study individual units, compare activation patterns across examples, or identify directions in the representation space that are associated with a behavior. These methods work with the model’s internal representation and do not require the final explanation to use a predefined concept vocabulary.

title: 8  Introduction
text:
8.2 Concept-based explainability
Concept-based explanations describe model behavior using properties that people can name and understand. For text, examples include contains a negation, mentions poor service, or uses positive language. A useful concept should have a clear meaning, be observable from the input, and be relevant to the task.
In supervised concept-based methods, the concept vocabulary is selected before training. Domain experts or dataset designers choose the concepts, and training examples are annotated with both task labels and concept values. This gives the explanation a fixed vocabulary, but its quality depends on whether that vocabulary is complete and consistently annotated.

8.2.1 Concepts and concept space
A concept is a property of an input. For this tutorial, we use \(c_j^\star(x)\) as an idealized value of concept \(j\) for input \(x\):
\[
c_j^\star : \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{C}_j,
\tag{8.1}\]
where \(\mathcal{X}\) is the input space and \(\mathcal{C}_j\) is the set of possible values for concept \(j\). A binary concept such as contains a negation has \(\mathcal{C}_j=\{0,1\}\). An ordinal concept such as sentiment strength could take values in \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). Concepts may also be categorical or continuous.
For \(k\) concepts, the concept space is
\[
\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}_1 \times \cdots \times \mathcal{C}_k.
\tag{8.2}\]
An input \(x\) is described by the concept vector
\[
\mathbf{c}^\star(x)
=\left(c_1^\star(x),\ldots,c_k^\star(x)\right)
\in \mathcal{C}.
\tag{8.3}\]
This is a modeling convention, not a claim that every concept has one objectively correct value. Real annotations are less certain. Annotators may disagree, a concept may be subjective, or the input may not contain enough information to determine its value. An observed annotation \(c_j\) should therefore be treated as a measurement of the intended concept, not necessarily as perfect ground truth. When uncertainty matters, a model can predict a distribution \(p(c_j\mid x)\) instead of a single value.

title: 8  Introduction
text:
8.3 Concept discovery
Concept discovery methods do not begin with a complete, annotated concept vocabulary. Instead, they search a model’s learned representations for recurring clusters, directions, or patterns that may correspond to meaningful properties. A person then interprets and validates the discovered patterns.
Concept discovery is closely related to concept-based explainability. It is treated as a separate family here because the concepts are learned from representations rather than fully specified before training. A discovered pattern should not be called a meaningful concept until its interpretation is supported across multiple examples and its relationship to model behavior has been tested.

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
text:
10.1 Architecture and inference
The original Concept Bottleneck Model formulation is a supervised concept-based method built around a human-defined concept vocabulary. The broader idea of concept-based explainability, including the definition of a concept and the notation used here, is introduced in the introduction.
A Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM) makes a prediction in two stages:
\[
x
\xrightarrow{\;g_\theta\;}
\widehat{\mathbf{c}}
\xrightarrow{\;f_\phi\;}
\widehat{y}.
\tag{10.1}\]
The concept predictor \(g_\theta\) maps the input to named concept values. The task predictor \(f_\phi\) then uses those values to predict the task output:
\[
h_{\theta,\phi}(x)=f_\phi\!\left(g_\theta(x)\right).
\tag{10.2}\]
The concept vector is called a bottleneck because it is the only information passed to the task predictor. In a strict CBM, there is no separate path from \(x\) to \(\widehat{y}\).
Each coordinate in \(\widehat{\mathbf{c}}\) has an assigned meaning. For a binary concept, \(\widehat{c}_j\) may be a hard value in \(\{0,1\}\), a score between 0 and 1, or a logit. A real-valued score gives the task predictor more graded information than a hard value. It should be interpreted as confidence only when the score has been calibrated. Categorical concepts are usually represented by one score per category, while continuous concepts can be represented directly.
The architecture of \(g_\theta\) depends on the input. It may be a convolutional network for images or a transformer for text. The task predictor is often smaller. For example, a linear predictor can assign a score to class \(r\):
\[
s_r(\widehat{\mathbf{c}})
=b_r+\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_{rj}\widehat{c}_j.
\tag{10.3}\]
Here, \(w_{rj}\) describes how concept \(j\) is associated with class \(r\) across the model, while \(w_{rj}\widehat{c}_j\) is that concept’s contribution to the class score for one example. Weight magnitudes can be compared directly only when the concept variables use comparable scales. These values describe the model’s calculation; they should not be interpreted as causal effects. A nonlinear task predictor can model interactions between concepts, but its decisions are harder to inspect.

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
text:
10.2 What does a CBM explain?
A CBM provides a concept-level account of the final prediction. For one input, a reader can inspect:

The model’s description of the input: which concepts were predicted and their predicted scores. A score represents confidence only when it is calibrated.
The task decision: which concepts supported or opposed the predicted class. This is easiest to see with a linear task predictor.
The sensitivity to corrections: whether the task prediction changes when an incorrect concept is replaced with a corrected value.

Across a dataset, the weights of a linear task predictor show which concepts are generally associated with each class. Concept accuracy can also be examined separately for each concept to find systematic errors.
The bottleneck does not make the whole system transparent. The concept predictor \(g_\theta\) may still be a complex neural network, so the CBM does not automatically explain why the input produced a particular concept score. It makes the second step, from concepts to the task prediction, easier to inspect.






NoteExample: classifying a restaurant review



Suppose a CBM predicts whether a customer recommends a restaurant. For the review “The pasta was excellent, but we waited an hour and will not return,” its concept predictor might produce:



Predicted concept
Score




Praises the food
0.94


Reports slow service
0.91


Intends to return
0.08



The task predictor combines these three scores to produce the recommendation label. This explanation is more informative than the label alone: it shows that the model detected both the positive comment about the food and the stronger negative signals about the overall experience. If one concept is wrong, it can be corrected and the task prediction can be recomputed.

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
text:
10.3 Training regimes
Suppose the training data contain triples \((x_i,\mathbf{c}_i,y_i)\). CBMs are commonly trained in one of three ways:

Independent training: train \(g_\theta\) to predict the annotated concepts, and separately train \(f_\phi\) using the annotated concepts as input. The task predictor therefore learns from clean annotations but receives predicted concepts at inference time. See Koh et al. (2020), Concept Bottleneck Models.
Sequential training: first train \(g_\theta\), freeze it, and then train \(f_\phi\) on \(g_\theta(x_i)\). The task predictor sees the kinds of concept errors it will encounter at inference time. See Koh et al. (2020), Concept Bottleneck Models.
Joint training: train both components together using a concept loss and a task loss. The task loss is backpropagated through both \(f_\phi\) and \(g_\theta\), while the concept loss keeps the bottleneck tied to the annotated concepts. See Koh et al. (2020), Concept Bottleneck Models.
A typical joint objective is
\[
\mathcal{L}
=\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{concept}}
  \left(g_\theta(x_i),\mathbf{c}_i\right)
+\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}
  \left(f_\phi(g_\theta(x_i)),y_i\right),
\tag{10.4}\]
where \(\lambda\) controls the importance of accurate concept prediction. Joint training can improve task performance, but it is still necessary to evaluate whether the predicted concepts match their intended meanings.
Sheth and Kahou (2023), Auxiliary Losses for Learning Generalizable Concept-based Models, extend joint training with cooperative-CBM (coop-CBM). Their method adds an auxiliary head that predicts the task label from the representation shared with the concept predictor. Its objective combines the concept loss, an auxiliary task loss, the final task loss, and a concept orthogonal loss. The orthogonal loss encourages within-concept similarity and separation between different concept representations. The auxiliary head helps shape the shared representation during training, while the final task predictor still receives only the predicted concepts. The paper evaluates the approach on image-classification datasets, including settings with distribution shift.

The concept loss must match the concept type. Binary concepts commonly use binary cross-entropy, categorical concepts use cross-entropy, and continuous concepts use a regression loss. If only some concepts are annotated for an example, the concept loss can be calculated over the available annotations.
crumbs: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
text:
10.4 Concept interventions
At inference time, a person can inspect \(\widehat{\mathbf{c}}\) and correct concepts that are clearly wrong. If \(S\) is the set of corrected concepts, define
\[
\widetilde{c}_j=
\begin{cases}
c_j^{\text{edit}}, & j\in S,\\
\widehat{c}_j, & j\notin S.
\end{cases}
\tag{10.5}\]
The revised prediction is \(\widetilde{y}=f_\phi(\widetilde{\mathbf{c}})\). This supports questions such as: Would the prediction change if the concept “contains a negation” were corrected from absent to present?
An intervention explains the behavior of the model under a concept edit. It does not prove that changing the corresponding property in the real world would cause the same outcome. Edits can also create unlikely combinations of concepts, so their results should be interpreted carefully.
crumbs: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
text:
10.5 Evaluating a CBM
Task accuracy alone is not enough. A useful evaluation should check four parts of the model:

Task performance: how accurately \(\widehat{y}\) predicts the task label.
Concept performance: how accurately each \(\widehat{c}_j\) predicts its annotated concept. Per-concept results are important because an average can hide a poorly learned concept.
Concept-set sufficiency: how well the task can be predicted from the annotated concepts. Poor performance may indicate that the vocabulary is missing useful information, but it can also result from noisy concept annotations or an unsuitable task predictor.
Intervention performance: how the task performance changes as incorrect concept predictions are corrected. This tests whether better concepts lead to better task predictions.

These measurements answer different questions. A CBM may predict the task well while predicting some concepts poorly. It may also predict every annotated concept well but perform poorly because the concept set is incomplete or the task predictor is unsuitable.
crumbs: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
text:
10.6 Limitations and appropriate use cases
CBMs are most useful when a task has a stable concept vocabulary, reliable concept annotations are available, and a person can meaningfully inspect or correct the concepts. They are particularly suitable when concept-level feedback is more practical than changing the original input.
Their main limitations are:

Incomplete vocabulary: if important information is missing from the concept set, a strict CBM may lose predictive accuracy.
Annotation cost and noise: concept labels can be expensive to collect and may differ across annotators.
Concept prediction errors: an understandable concept is not useful when the model predicts it unreliably.
Hidden shortcuts: the concept predictor may use an unintended input pattern to predict the correct concept value.
Information in soft scores: small variations in continuous concept scores can carry information beyond the concepts’ stated meanings. This can weaken interpretability and concept interventions, as discussed by Havasi et al. (2022).
Limited transparency with complex heads: a nonlinear \(f_\phi\) may make the relationship between concepts and predictions difficult to follow.

Architectures with residual features or a direct path from \(x\) to \(\widehat{y}\) may recover some accuracy. However, because named concepts no longer carry all the information used for the prediction, they do not provide the same explanation guarantee as a strict CBM.
crumbs: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models

title: 10  Method A: Concept Bottleneck Models
section: 10.7 Reducing the need for concept annotations
text:
10.7 Reducing the need for concept annotations
Recent extensions reduce the amount of per-example concept labeling. Label-free CBMs use a chosen list of concept names together with pretrained representations to construct a concept bottleneck without manually labeling every training example. Post-hoc CBMs project a pretrained model’s representations into a concept space rather than training the entire model from the beginning.
The term label-free refers to concept labels: these methods can still require task labels, a human-selected concept vocabulary, and pretrained models. Their concept scores must also be validated. A concept name alone does not guarantee that the score consistently measures the intended property.






TipKey takeaway



A strict CBM predicts named concepts first and makes the final prediction only from those concepts. This structure makes concept inspection and correction possible. The explanation is useful only when the concept vocabulary is relevant and the predicted concept values are reliable.

16.4.1 Visualization-Based Approaches
State-value heatmaps can reveal an agent’s strategic understanding of the environment. This is particularly useful in navigation-based settings such as mazes.
For more fine-grained explanations, we can also visualize state-action values (Q values) to identify the agent’s understanding of actions from the perspective of a given state.
Visiualization-based explainability toolkits for RL have been proposed such as DQNViz (Wang et al. 2018), developed for DQN-based agents learning Atari games.

Decision trees are inherently interpretable. Once a policy is learned, the reasoning behind every decision can be clearly traced by following the tree’s decision nodes. A recent focus in the RL community is using world models for better sample-efficiency and higher performance. By having a world model learn the environment dynamics \(P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)\), we can predict future states without interaction with the real environment. This is essential for planning and also has the useful side effect that it enables counterfactual reasoning, useful for generating “what-if” scenarios.

title: 17  Pertubation-Based Saliency Maps for RL
text:
Method: Pertubation-based saliency maps
The core idea behind this method is to measure how much a neural network’s output (its policy and value estimates) changes when information is selectively removed from the input image. Rather than simply blacking out a region, the method introduces spatial uncertainty by locally blurring the image. If the agent’s proposed action or value estimate drastically changes when a specific area is blurred, that region is highly salient to the agent’s decision-making process.
The perturbation applied to a localized coordinate \((i,j)\) on an image frame \(I_t\) is defined by the following key math:
\[\Phi(I_t,i,j)=\underbrace{I_t}_{\text{image frame}}\odot (1-\underbrace{M(i,j)}_{\text{mask}})+\underbrace{A(I_t,\sigma_A)}_{\text{blurred frame}}\odot M(i,j),\]
where \(\odot\) denotes the Hadamard product and \(I_{1:t}\) is a sequence of images.
This visualization technique is separate from the RL algorithm used for training. The authors used the A3C algorithm, which yields both a policy and value function. The above procedure for constructing pertubation-based saliency was applied to both the policy \(\pi\) and \(V^\pi\). They use patches of 5x5 pixels to reduce the required computation.

title: 22  Introduction
text: Explainable multi-agent systems (XMAS) refers to the subfield of artificial intelligence that integrates LLM explainability methods within multi-agent AI systems (MAS). This recently established field of study addresses the emergent behaviours of MAS, which derive from the added complexity of multi-agent settings. As single-agent AI systems become progressively more commercialized (finance, e-commerce, legal services), the natural step towards MAS necessitates the corresponding MAS-specific explainability methods.

title: 23  What are agents?
text:
Generally, agents refer to any entity capable of perceiving its environment and taking action (Cheng et al. 2024).  Namely, large language model (LLM) based agents leverage the natural language processing capabilities of LLMs (complex reasoning, text summarization, machine translation) (Qin et al. 2026)  , while attempting to address their fundamental limitations: (Plaat et al. 2025; Liu and Shu 2025)



Hallucination The tendency of LLMs to produce plausible yet factually unsupported content, deriving from data misinformation, pre-training biases, and over-confidence, among others. (Huang et al. 2025) 
Training data LLM intelligence is limited by the data available during training, which causes struggles in factual accuracy and failure to adapt to new situations.
Reasoning Although LLMs continue to impress in natural language processing, model reasoning remains a well-reported challenge as LLMs are designed to predict the most probable next words, rather than making logically sound claims.
Prompt Engineering LLMs are sensitive to minor details in prompts, making prompt improvement a tedious, manual task. (Plaat et al. 2025) 


Consequently, the architecture of LLM-based agents adds four fundamental modules absent from LLMs: (Wang et al. 2023)
Profile: The identity, role, tendencies, and constraints that define an agent and lead to better, grounded decisions.
Memory: The persistent system by which agents retain, refine, and recall information while accumulating knowledge.
Planning: The module that decomposes complex, high-level plans into sub-tasks for a simplified sequence of actions.
Action: The tools that enable an agent to translate internal decisions into external executions.

Some authors argue for a fifth module evolution, describing how agents progressively enhance their intelligence through self-reflection. (Li et al. 2024)
Analogously, agents can be understood as being proactive whereas LLMs are reactive. Rather, LLMs predict and agents reason, act and interact. (Plaat et al. 2025) 
By adopting a proactive stance, LLM-based agents address the constraints of models by integrating a model within an architectural loop with distinct modules that handle it’s limitations. (Liu and Shu 2025; Plaat et al. 2025)  
Implementations of agent-based systems have rapidly evolved into a variety of industries, (arguably) justifying it’s position as the current paradigm in machine learning research. Such areas include healthcare (medical diagnosis (J. Chen et al. 2025), cardiology (Zhou et al. 2024), therapeutic counseling (Steenstra and Bickmore 2025)), research (survey generation (Liang et al. 2025), scientific discovery (Gottweis and Natarajan 2025)), and software engineering (coding reasoning (H.-Y. Chen et al. 2025), code generation (Endla et al. 2025)). The term agent has even become a buzzword within the tech industry, often being misused by marketing teams to excite unbeknownst customers, reflecting the prominence of single-agent systems. (Cheng et al. 2024; Ferrag et al. 2026) 










But as the scopes and complexities of single-agent implementations grow, the more difficult is it for an agent to navigate more dynamic, complex scenarios. An underlying assumption within an abundance of single-agent implementations is static, closed environments, which, of course, is a reductive representation of nuanced, real-world scenarios. (Qi et al. 2026; Pan and Wu 2025; Feng et al. 2026)




23.0.1 What are multi-agent systems?
Multi-agent systems (MAS) are systems that enclose multiple autonomous LLM-based agents to enable more complex reasoning, problem-solving, and simulation. Leveraging collective judgment is a natural step in the evolution of agentic AI, addressing the simplistic assumed environments of single-agent systems. As singular agents reach limits in complexity, they may relapse to the initial pitfalls of LLMs (hallucination, limits of reasoning). Containing multiple agents in a cohesive framework allows for dynamic collaboration, flexibility, and emergent collective intelligence. (Guo et al. 2024; Pan and Wu 2025) As Aristotle argued, “a feast to which many contribute is better than a dinner provided out of a single purse”. (Aristotle 1885)



Unlike the evolution of reactive LLMs to proactive LLM-based agents, the progression of single-agent systems to multi-agent systems is more so a re-contextualization than an evolution. Multi-agent systems typically avoid heavily altering the architecture of single-agents, rather enabling it’s modules (profiling, memory, planning, action) to adequately handle a multi-agent context through inter-agent means. (Guo et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024)
Notably, agents within MAS are more specialized; agent profiles can, for example, contain human personas (Park et al. 2023) or possess knowledge limited to specific disciplines (Tang et al. 2024) to simulate real-world contexts or solve complex tasks. Similarly, planning modules and action modules are equipped with unique mechanisms that address multi-agent complexity, namely, task decomposition and collaborative feedback loops for planning (Li et al. 2025), and environmental interaction for action. Memory modules extend further: hybrid memory provides agents with shared memory, capturing emergent collective intelligence. (Wu and Shu 2026) More exhaustive, MAS architecture surveys elaborate on the methodologies used to handle MAS complexities in distributed knowledge, coordination, communication, among others. (Guo et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024)





Beyond refactoring single-agent architectures, orchestration represents the novel mechanisms by which agents are integrated within an MAS, re-contextualizing agents to adequately perform under more complex and nuanced scenarios. (Adimulam et al. 2026; Zhou et al. 2026)
Orchestration can be understood as the structured coordination and collaboration of enclosed agents. (Adimulam et al. 2026)  Orchestration is defined by three key dimensions, organizational structure, communication mechanism, and collaboration pattern, through which various MAS can address unique use cases. (Adimulam et al. 2026; Zhou et al. 2026)
Organizational Structure: Defined as the interaction topology of the MAS, which outlines how authority is divided and which agents interact directly . Among others, some structures are:
Hierarchical: A pyramidal chain, akin to a traditional top-down business model. Higher tier agents interact with agents immediately below them, who subsequently continue the chain of command.
Decentralized: Agents communicate with other agents directly, removing any need for a central coordinator. Uniquely, every agent is able to coordinate with any other agent.
Flat Collaborative: Authority is distributed among all agents, but any agent can only communicate with those near it.
Communication Mechanism: Procedures and protocols used to transmit and synchronize information, including intent, observations, and tasks. Some forms include:
Direct Channels: Communication by which information is explicitly relayed towards another agent, or a group of agents.
Indirect Channels: Receivers and senders are not explicitly determined during communication, rather, communication involves modifying a shared state.
Collaboration Pattern: The methodologies by which agents sequence tasks, distribute responsibilities, and provide feedback. An MAS collaboration pattern defines how each agent works together, utilizing it’s structure and communication methods. The key dimensions are the following.
Collaborative intent: The relationship between the agents’ objectives, defining whether agents pursue a shared positive-sum objective, or mutually competing on a micro-level for a macro-level, aligned goal.
Collaborative workflows: The process through which information and tasks are advanced among agents, ranging from feed-forward pipelines, or parallel, aggregation.
Collaborative protocols: The standards that define interactions for communication. (Zhou et al. 2026)

Orchestration has been proven to be a necessary aspect for scalable MAS, preventing drawbacks such as conflicting goals, circular reasoning, or inconsistent memories which emerge from evolving past single-agent systems. Combined with re-contextualized agent architectures, orchestration helps MAS tackle real-world, complex tasks. (Dextra Labs 2026) 


23.0.2 Why is explainability in multi-agent systems necessary?
The autonomy and powerful reasoning of agentic systems can easily be seen as a century-defining technology, grasping at the possibilities of superhuman cognitive ability. However, the excitement behind agentic AI, including the growing academic research and commercialization, may be propagating its inherent opacity, the fatal flaw of agentic systems. In the general scope of LLMs, the rapidly growing gap between the ability to interpret models and the widespread usage of these models is called the explainability crisis. (Decision Physics 2026)

The difficulty of interpreting LLMs (as discussed in previous chapters) can be attributed to its opaque systems. As a result, agentic systems that inherit LLMs as fundamental mechanisms would inherit a potentially unintelligible model. Multi-agent systems amplifies this effect by introducing new dimensions to agentic systems, complicating explainability moreover. The most notable reasons are: 

Distributed information obscures attribution: Information parsed and refined between multiple agents in systematic procedures distorts the interpretability of intentions, decisions, and behaviours by introducing layers of abstraction.
Cascading errors and behaviours among agents: The degradation of communication introduces errors and unwanted behaviours that cascades into system-level effects, making failure attribution difficult. (Tanveer 2026)



The orchestration layer introduces complexity: Orchestration, beyond adding structural integrity and coordination, also adds a layer of complexity that disrupts causal attribution. (Adimulam et al. 2026; Zhou et al. 2026)

Although the explainability crisis may be generally applicable to the broader scope of black-box models, multi-agent systems experience this effect amplified. Concerns raise as MAS emerge as viable options to SAS, as to address more specialized challenges.
Notably, Anthropic utilizes MAS in the Claude Research feature, arguing for it’s effectiveness in open-ended research questions. (Hadfield et al. 2025) The idea that the gradual commercialization of MAS necessitates explainability is greater than the field of ML; after all, any technology implemented without systemic understanding seems to be unethical.
